children: India’s artisans create luxury, Indian consumers fund it, but foreign brands capture much of the prestige, pricing power and premium

India exports the ingredients of luxury and imports its symbols. Its artisans produce textiles, jewellery and objects of extraordinary refinement, often drawing on skills perfected over generations. Yet the brands that command the greatest prestige among affluent Indians are overwhelmingly international. India is acquiring the wealth to consume luxury faster than it is building the institutions to own it.
The country that creates the craft still imports the cachet.

Kearney estimates that India’s luxury market, valued at USD 7.74 billion in 2023, could approach USD 12 billion by 2028. A Crux study of 2025 estimates USD 16 billion by 2030. But the expansion of a market does not necessarily translate into the creation of domestic luxury businesses. The distinction lies in who owns the brands, controls distribution and captures the premium.
Luxury Is An Industry, Not A Price Tag

Luxury is an economic architecture, not simply an expensive product. Design, scarcity and craftsmanship create desirability; reputation, distribution and customer loyalty convert it into pricing power. The artisan may produce the embroidery, weave or gemstone setting, while another enterprise owns the label, controls the retail experience and captures the larger commercial premium.
The hands that create distinction rarely own the price of distinction.

This is not an argument that Indian artisans lack skill or that foreign brands contribute nothing. International luxury houses create employment, transfer capabilities, and invest in retail. The imbalance lies in ownership. A country can supply exceptional workmanship to global brands for decades without developing the intellectual property, customer data and commercial institutions that make those brands valuable.

India’s craft economy illustrates the difference between value creation and value capture. A handwoven textile may be unique, but without consistent quality, working capital, design ownership and access to affluent customers, its producer remains dependent on intermediaries. Cultural inheritance creates an advantage; it does not automatically create a business.
From Craft To Commerce: What Italy Built

Italy’s luxury strength rests on more than aesthetic heritage. Specialist manufacturers, family enterprises, designers and global houses connect production to international demand. This industrial structure turns regional craftsmanship into globally recognised products, supported by quality standards, distribution and pricing power.

Japan offers a different lesson. Its 1974 Traditional Craft Industries Promotion Act links craft recognition to successor training, product development and demand creation. Heritage is treated as productive capital requiring investment, skills and commercial discipline. Neither country is a template India can simply reproduce. Their histories differ. Yet both demonstrate why cultural wealth cannot generate economic value at scale without industrial infrastructure.

India has an example of this transition. In 2021, Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail acquired a 51 per cent stake in Sabyasachi for Rs 398 crore. The designer’s first international flagship opened in New York in 2022. Capital and commercial infrastructure helped extend a Kolkata-founded design house into international retail.

Sabyasachi demonstrates possibility, not completion. India needs more enterprises across fashion, jewellery, accessories and lifestyle that can sustain global demand while protecting their distinctiveness.
Heritage supplies the distinction. Industrial infrastructure determines who captures its value.
India’s Luxury Boom Has An Ownership Problem

India’s opportunity is arriving as the global luxury industry reassesses its economics. Consumers are questioning price increases and placing greater weight on experiences, provenance, personal relevance and service. India has natural assets in hospitality, wellness, architecture, food and regional design. But cultural authenticity alone cannot command a premium. It must translate into consistent quality, distinctive products and customer relationships that endure.

The domestic market faces a physical constraint. Reuters reported in March 2026 that India had only three true luxury malls, against approximately 110 million square feet of Grade A mall space nationally, compared with 400 million in China. This shortage has complicated expansion plans for international brands.

The constraint extends beyond real estate. Luxury requires controlled distribution, presentation and service. Without suitable locations and reliable routes from production to purchase, brands cannot sustain a consistent customer experience.
A Bigger Market Does Not Make A Stronger Brand

India’s luxury market may expand rapidly. But market growth measures consumers’ purchasing power, not domestic brands’ economic power. The opportunity lies in converting rising consumption into Indian-owned brands, pricing power and enduring commercial value.

India’s central risk is to confuse the growth of its luxury market with the creation of a luxury industry. The two can move together, but they need not. Consumers may spend more on imported labels while domestic producers remain concentrated in contract manufacturing, occasion-led sales or fragmented craft markets.
The Real Prize Is Pricing Power

Scaling presents its own dilemma. Excessive standardisation can erase the scarcity that supports a premium; refusing to modernise can leave artisans economically unviable. The task is to build enterprises that protect design integrity while professionalising production, distribution and customer management.

India’s luxury ambition should be measured not only by market size, but by the number of Indian-owned brands with global customers, durable pricing power and a meaningful share of value retained by domestic creators.

The distinction is ultimately between a country that produces desirable objects and one that owns the institutions that make them valuable. India has the former in abundance. The latter remains scarce.
If India fails to close that gap, its artisans will continue to create the distinction, its consumers will continue to finance it, and other countries will continue to own the premium.
